[Test][BugFix] Align bisect dependencies with hardware Dockerfiles (#20919)

### What this PR does / why we need it?

The nightly bisect tool previously adapted dependencies from a partial
set of version and requirement files. On A3, that led it to fetch
`torch-npu` from a slow or unreachable package source and misclassify
environment setup failures as model regressions.

This change reads each candidate's hardware-specific base Dockerfile
(A2, A3, 310P, or A5), its matching nightly Dockerfile,
`requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, and `requirements-nightly.txt`.
The bisect tool uses the selected build recipe to switch vLLM, vLLM
Ascend, nightly dependencies, Dockerfile-installed wheels,
flash-attention-npu, and AISBench in build order. It rejects CANN image
changes and unsupported Dockerfile build-step changes as environment
errors.

The new single-node `--mock-tests` mode performs the same checkout,
version adaptation, dependency installation, and rebuild steps as a real
trial, then simulates only the pytest verdict. Mock runs use separate
state and reports, mark every verdict as simulated, and do not claim a
first bad commit. Per-round logs record the requested Dockerfile pairing
and installed vLLM/torch-npu versions before and after preparation. The
PyTorch CPU extra index remains as specified by the Dockerfile; a
reachable Huawei Cloud PyPI mirror is used as the primary index for
isolated build dependencies.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. It changes dependency adaptation behavior and adds a
developer-facing bisect CLI flag. No model inference API changes. This
is tooling-only, so no release note fragment is required by AGENTS.md.

[Performance] drop redundant contiguous copy and zero-fill in engram lookup (#19368)

### What this PR does / why we need it?
`AscendParallelEngramEmbedding.embed_gathered` no longer forces a
`.contiguous()` copy of the per-layer hash slice and no longer primes
the gather output with `torch.zeros` (a full-buffer fill). Output
storage is allocated with `torch.empty`.
The gather kernels already walk `ids` with an explicit token stride
(`ids.stride(0)`) and only require a unit inner stride -- which the
per-layer slice of the contiguous `[tokens, layers, columns]` hash
buffer already has, so the contiguous copy was dead weight. The kernels
also write every output row and store zeroes for out-of-range ids, so
zero-priming the output is redundant by contract.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?
NO.

### How was this patch tested?
- Served DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-W4A8 (TP8, `--engram-config cpu_offload`,
INT8 + MXFP8 mixed storage): single-request torch-profiler trace shows
the per-layer `contiguous` copy and `zeros` fill kernels gone from the
lookup window in steady-state decode steps.

[BugFix][WeightTransfer] Import each packed NPU IPC export once (#20740)

### What this PR does / why we need it?

Packed NPU IPC transfers currently rebuild and then release the
producer's shared mapping once per chunk. The producer, however, exports
its reusable staging buffer only once and sends the same rebuild
arguments with every chunk. Since torch pairs one IPC export with one
consumer rebuild/release cycle, a multi-chunk transfer drives the
producer-side refcount negative. Once the staging buffer is dropped, it
cannot be reclaimed, leaking one `packed_buffer_size_bytes` allocation
per update on every producer rank.

This adapts the import-cache fix merged upstream in vLLM
[#51259](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51259) to the Ascend
NPU consumer:

- add an NPU implementation of the upstream `PackedBufferImporter` that
reuses one rebuilt mapping across chunks from the same export;
- wire one importer into each `NPUIPCWeightTransferEngine` and release
it through the inherited `finish_weight_update()` / `shutdown()`
lifecycle or when a new export replaces it;
- add regression coverage for one import across multiple chunks, fresh
payload reads through the cached mapping, cleanup, reuse after cleanup,
replacement between exports, and a failed rebuild;
- update the existing receive test to assert that the engine passes its
shared importer to the packed consumer.

The unpacked path, wire format, public APIs and configuration are
unchanged. This is a focused alternative to the importer portion of the
broader, currently conflicting
[#18085](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/pull/18085), not a
replacement for that PR.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. Packed NPU IPC live weight updates no longer retain a producer
staging buffer after each update. There is no new API or configuration.
A release-note fragment is included.

### How was this patch tested?

- CPU source harness with the real engine, importer, packing and loading
code; only configuration, logging and hardware primitives were stubbed:
**125 passed**.
- The same regression case against the pre-fix source fails at the
second import with `2 != 1`, confirming it covers the reported
lifecycle.
- Eight-card Ascend host (225), real eight-layer BF16 checkpoint,
TP4/DP2/EP8, eight producer ranks, packed buffer 4352 MiB,
`max_tokens=8`:
  - structured run report: **passed**;
- both `/v1/completions` and `/v1/chat/completions`: **4/4** outputs,
tokens and finite token logprobs identical before and after the packed
weight update, **8/8 total**;
- checkpoint manifest and sampled parameters were consistent across the
eight workers;
- the update client exit did not reproduce `Producer process has been
terminated before all shared NPU tensors released`.
- Ruff check, Ruff format check, `py_compile` and `git diff --check`
passed.

The real-host run completed the update and post-update inference checks.
Normal post-update service shutdown was not completed because the
shared-host occupancy guard detected unrelated NPU processes and stopped
the test container; that shutdown path remains covered by the unit
regression but was not exercised end to end in that run.

### Checklist

#### Testing

- [x] **Boundary / edge-case coverage:** Repeated chunks,
replace-on-next-export, repeated cleanup and a failed rebuild are
covered.
- [x] **Regression test:** The new test fails against the pre-fix
source.
- [x] **Error / failure path coverage:** A rebuild failure preserves the
existing mapping, which is released by cleanup.
- [x] **Meaningful & reliable tests:** Tests exercise the actual
importer lifecycle and payload freshness rather than only checking call
counts.
- [ ] **Performance impact:** This removes repeated IPC opens and
closes; no standalone benchmark was run.

[Doc] Drop --dtype from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B A2/A3 w8a8 example (#21559)

### What this PR does / why we need it?

The Qwen3.6-35B-A3B tutorial ("A2 Series / A3 Series" deployment tab)
forces `--dtype float16` for the `Eco-Tech/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-w8a8`
checkpoint. On Atlas 800I A3/A2 the CANN A8W8 quantized-matmul kernels
(`aclnnGroupedMatmulWeightNz`, `aclnnQuantMatmulWeightNz`) only accept
FP32/BF16 scales, not FP16. With `--dtype float16` the W8A8 scale
tensors are created in FP16 and the engine fails during the profile run
with aclnn error 161002 / E1001:

```
AcLNN Parameter Error(E1001): In op [grouped matmul], the data types of [scale] mismatched,
the reason is: [scale[0] dtype FLOAT16 and y dtype FLOAT16 are not supported when A8W8 per-token quant].
RuntimeError: npu_grouped_matmul ... call aclnnGroupedMatmulWeightNz failed, error code is 161002
```

at `vllm_ascend/quantization/methods/w8a8/w8a8_dynamic.py::apply_gmm2`.

This PR drops the `--dtype float16` line from the A2/A3 example so it
keeps the model's native `bfloat16` dtype (from the model config, no
override needed), and updates the parameter description accordingly
(`float16` is required only on Atlas 300I DUO). The Atlas 300I DUO
example (FP16-only platform) is unchanged.

Fixes #21532. Related: #12907 / #12919 (same root cause fixed for the
Qwen3.5/3.6-27B tutorials), #20702 (runtime fix that casts
grouped-matmul scales to FP32).

[Feature][KV Pool] Support GLM RecoverSSM prefix reuse with PCP (#20835) ### What this PR does / why we need it? Enable GLM-5.3-Flash RecoverSSM to reuse aligned prefill checkpoints through AscendStore bulk and layerwise transfers, including KDA head shards owned by different PCP ranks. **RecoverSSM support** - Enable GLM-5.3-Flash RecoverSSM to reuse aligned prefill checkpoints through AscendStore bulk and layerwise transfers. - Export persistent convolution/recurrent state using model-declared Mamba copy functions; keep temporary verification records local. - Remove the RecoverSSM connector-name allowlist, including its rejection of MultiConnector, while retaining existing execution constraints and model-specific checks. **Mamba PCP support in AscendStore KVPool** - Currently reject simultaneous TP>1 and PCP>1 during AscendStore connector initialization whenever sharded Mamba groups are present. Remove this validation after mamba joint TP * PCP head partitioning is implemented. - In bulk mode, use TP-major/PCP-minor ranks (tp_rank * pcp_size + pcp_rank) for sharded Mamba state keys. Every state partition saves every eligible checkpoint instead of distributing checkpoint candidates across PCP ranks; a prefix hit requires all partitions. Keep the existing attention and TP-replicated state key paths. - In layerwise mode, both Memcache and Mooncake keep the original TP state rank and add @pcp_size:@pcp_rank: only for sharded Mamba groups. When DCP=1, replicated attention groups share one key across PCP ranks; PCP rank 0 saves using the existing TP writer selection, and every PCP worker can load that object. With DCP>1, preserve the existing save-leader and align-state selection. For TP=1/PCP=2, the two KDA workers own different head states. The original bulk path can give both workers the same key and divide checkpoint candidates between them; a checkpoint can then appear complete with only half of its state. The bulk key format remains: ``` @dcp:@head_or_tp_rank:@pp_rank:@group:@cache_role:@cache_family:@ ``` For sharded Mamba state, `` changes from `tp_rank to tp_rank * pcp_size + pcp_rank`: ``` Before: PCP rank 0 → head_or_tp_rank:0 PCP rank 1 → head_or_tp_rank:0 After: PCP rank 0 → head_or_tp_rank:0 PCP rank 1 → head_or_tp_rank:1 ``` This change gives each state shard its own key, saves both at every eligible boundary, and requires both keys before restoring each worker's corresponding state. In layerwise mode, Memcache previously used the same TP-only key for different PCP state shards, allowing them to overwrite the same allocation. Keep the original TP rank and append PCP coordinates only for sharded Mamba groups. When DCP=1, replicated attention keeps one shared key, with PCP rank 0 saving it. DCP>1 retains the existing save-owner behavior. Mooncake follows the same distinction, also avoiding duplicate attention KV objects across PCP ranks. ### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change? Yes. GLM RecoverSSM can reuse aligned checkpoints through `AscendStoreConnector` with Memcache or Mooncake, in bulk or layerwise mode. RecoverSSM still requires PP=1 and DCP=1. [Feature] Add Mooncake V2 layerwise push connector (#20940)

### What this PR does / why we need it?

Add an experimental Ascend Mooncake V2 layerwise push path alongside the
existing pull connector. D allocates destination KV blocks and publishes
request routing through the Ascend layerwise proxy's metaserver. P
discovers D cache layouts from the D scheduler metadata service and
submits layer WRITE batches through a thread pool.

- Track outstanding WRITE futures per destination engine. Ordinary layer
hooks accumulate ready layers while that engine is busy; the last layer
attempts to flush the backlog and queues DONE after the request's
submitted WRITE dependencies.
- Keep `wait_for_save` as the step barrier and fallback for late
metadata, caches without layer hooks, and connector-only steps. D
aggregates producer-rank completions before reporting receive success or
failure to the scheduler.
- Reuse common metadata and Mamba address calculation. Handle chunked
prefill, cached prefixes, multiple cache groups per physical layer, TP
head partitions/replicas, and final-chunk-only SWA/circular/Mamba state
transfers. Exclude speculative Mamba tail blocks from P transfer
metadata.
- Convert WRITE errors into request-level error DONE without raising
them into the model thread. Cancellation before first worker dispatch
carries D completion endpoints and needs no cache discovery;
cancellation after dispatch preserves existing WRITE dependencies.

This draft is developed against the paired vLLM layerwise work in
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62504. Native WRITE calls are
assumed to return within the configured transport timeout (30 seconds in
the current target environment); `wait_for_save` drains submitted tasks.
The connector contract treats a synchronous WRITE return, including an
error return, as completion of all host/device accesses. Violations of
that contract belong to the Mooncake/HIXL backend; no additional
post-return drain protocol is planned in this connector.

Current scope requires DCP=1 and no P request preemption. KVPP is
outside the support plan and is not a future implementation TODO.
Existing layout/topology guards remain in force; full model/topology
support is not established by host tests.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

Yes. Select `MooncakePushConnector` on both P and D, with `kv_role` set
to `kv_producer` and `kv_consumer`, respectively. `MooncakeConnectorV2`
remains the pull alias.

Includes release note fragment `release_notes/fragments/20940.yaml`.

### TODO / remaining work

#### Functional follow-ups

- [ ] **DCP support**: implement DCP sequence/rank mapping and
completion accounting. DCP > 1 is currently rejected.
- [ ] **P preemption and resume**: retire old transfers before source
blocks are reused, and rebuild transfer progress for resumed
allocations. Ordinary request abort, including abort before first worker
dispatch, is already implemented.
- [ ] **Metaserver batch progress**: acknowledge metadata acceptance
separately from P completion. Currently each POST occupies one of 32
threads until P finishes; a multi-prompt batch needing more than 32
metadata submissions through one D engine can wait on its own queued
submissions until timeout. Increasing the pool size alone does not
remove this dependency.

#### Validation still required before merge

- [ ] **Real NPU correctness**: verify actual WRITE payloads and event
ordering, early/final-layer DONE, cancellation, chunk boundaries and
prefix hits; cover supported TP/PCP/PP combinations, mixed cache groups,
graph execution and speculative/stateful model paths. These are
validation gaps, not claims of implemented support for every
combination.
- [ ] **Performance**: measure throughput, TTFT/TPOT and thread-pool
contention against the reference layerwise flow; host tests do not
establish a speedup.

### How was this patch tested?

- At commit `49c3bad3a`, **92 host-isolated tests passed** across
connector, push-scheduler, push-worker and push-sending tests. The local
harness extracts the actual scheduler/worker classes with framework/NPU
initialization isolated. Protocol checks use real HTTP/ZMQ sockets;
WRITE/event checks use mocks, with CPU byte-copy checks for address
mapping. This is not a full package-import or NPU E2E result.
- Consolidated duplicate abort/completion tests and equivalent input
variants; retained protocol, byte-copy and concurrency regressions.
Batch failure and pending-prefix progress now use normal inputs/hooks
instead of mutating unrelated internal state.
- Covered metadata discovery and retry, chunk boundaries, cached
prefixes, per-engine submission gating, final-layer backlog flushing,
out-of-order WRITE completion, request failure propagation, multi-rank
completion, pre-dispatch abort without cache discovery, cancellation
waiting for submitted WRITE, and Mamba speculative-tail exclusion.
- Ruff lint/format checks and `git diff --check` passed for the modified
implementation/tests.
- Targeted mypy 1.11.1 (the repository-pinned version) passed for all 11
Mooncake source files and, in a separate pass, all 13 Mooncake UT files.
Checks used installed pyzmq 27.3.0, msgspec and test dependencies with
`--follow-imports skip --ignore-missing-imports --check-untyped-defs
--python-version 3.11`. Both source and UT pyzmq export errors were
reproduced before the fixes. Other missing framework/NPU dependencies
remain ignored locally; this is not full-dependency CI validation.
- CI run
[42224301945](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-ascend/actions/runs/42224301945)
at `d5e67b555` passed pre-commit and mypy for Python 3.10/3.11/3.12.
Both CPU UT matrices reported the same 27 scheduler fixture setup
errors: the UT accessed `base_scheduler.FullAttentionSpec`, which the
production module does not export. Commit `49c3bad3a` imports cache
specs directly from `vllm.v1.kv_cache_interface`. The local harness was
also corrected to stop exporting unimported cache-spec mocks: it
reproduced all 27 errors before the UT fix, then passed all 92 tests
after it. Targeted mypy for all 13 Mooncake UT files and Ruff passed;
full CPU CI for the new commit is pending. Local pre-commit remains
intentionally skipped at the user's request. No NPU correctness or
performance run has been completed for this revision.

[Performance] Overlap PCP prefill communication and reduce KDA output collectives (#20454)

### What this PR does / why we need it?

PCP prefill needs to exchange main-KV and KPool inputs across ranks.
Waiting for these AllGathers before running independent query
projections leaves communication on the critical path. KDA also reduces
the full output on every PCP rank before selecting only that rank's
token rows.

This PR reduces those exposed waits and redundant output communication:

- **Main-KV overlap:** launch the PCP AllGather before MLA query
projections and wait when the gathered values are needed for the cache
write. Use one `exec_kv` path for immediate and deferred completion,
with DCP slot selection in one entry point. Offload accepts the same
signature while completing its existing cache writes and CPU commits
synchronously. Keep the send buffers alive until communication
completes.
- **KPool overlap and gather ordering:** start the hidden-state
AllGather before MLA/indexer query computation and restore token order
at the KPool consumer. Keep contiguous send buffers alive until the
consumer waits for completion. In native SFA preprocessing, enqueue
main-KV and KPool gathers before output-projection weight/scale gathers,
whose results are consumed later.
- **KDA ReduceScatter:** pack output rows by PCP ownership and replace
AllReduce followed by local row selection with ReduceScatter, so each
rank receives its own reduced rows. Preserve the existing SP and other
fallback paths.

The changes preserve token ordering, padding, replicated decode
prefixes, cache-write semantics, and graph-owned output buffers.
Ordinary sparse indexers retain their original K/scale gather and
cache-write pipeline.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

The communication optimizations activate automatically on the applicable
PCP paths. No new user-facing options are introduced. Release note:
`release_notes/fragments/20454.yaml`.

### How was this patch tested?

**Performance — long-prompt prefill**

AISBench synthetic fixed-token workload on GLM-5.3-Flash, measured
before the final KV entry-point refactor:

- **131,072 input tokens and 1 output token per request; 200 requests at
client concurrency 200**, using non-streaming responses.
- Each request has **117,504 cached input tokens and 13,568 newly
computed tokens**. Both variants use the same input token sequences and
cache-hit counts.
- Each variant starts from a fresh service load, primes the shared
prefix, and runs one 200-request warmup before one measured 200-request
batch. Preparation and warmup are excluded from the results.

| Metric | Baseline | PR | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Mean TTFT | 48.367578 s | 46.376675 s | −4.12% |
| Input token throughput | 276,079.40 tokens/s | 287,386.83 tokens/s |
+4.10% |

Both benchmark environments included the same external FP8 startup
compatibility patch. Both sides completed **200/200 requests with zero
preemption**. AISBench results were independently checked against all
per-request timing records. For this non-streaming, one-output-token
case, AISBench TTFT equals request latency. Input throughput counts all
input tokens, including cache hits.

**GPQA-Diamond — reasoning accuracy**

The full **198-question multiple-choice dataset** is scored with
AISBench's zero-shot CoT prompt, answer extraction, and GPQA evaluator.
The PR evaluation uses **client concurrency 32** and an output limit of
**131,072 tokens per question**, with normal EOS stopping.

| Metric | Baseline | PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Correct / total | 180 / 198 | 181 / 198 |
| Accuracy | 90.9091% | 91.4141% |
| Successful requests | 198 / 198 | 198 / 198 |

commits.message:
[Performance][MRV2] Optimize _penalties_kernel vocab grid to cut scalar overhead (#18613)

### What this PR does / why we need it?

`apply_penalties` launches `_penalties_kernel` on a 2-D grid
`(num_tokens, vocab_grid_size)`, where the second axis was sized as:

```python
vocab_grid_size = min(num_vocab_blocks, 65535 // num_tokens)
```

With Qwen3's vocabulary (151936) and `BLOCK_SIZE = 4096` there are 38
vocab blocks, and `65535 // num_tokens >= 38` for every `num_tokens <=
1724`. The expression therefore evaluates to **38 at every batch size we
actually serve**, i.e. one program per vocab block, and the grid-stride
loop inside the kernel never iterates. Each program pays the per-program
cost once for a single block of work.

That cost is not bandwidth. The kernel is **scalar-bound on A2**:
profiling `glm-5.3-flash-w8a8` with `AiCMetrics.PipeUtilization`, a
representative launch at logits `[8, 154880]` spends 83 % of its
vector-core time in the scalar pipe and 11 % in the vector pipe. Running
a fixed shape in fp32 instead of bf16 moves 1.5× the bytes and costs
**+0.15 %** time, which rules out bandwidth. The scalar unit also
dispatches to every other pipe, so per-program scalar work serialises
everything behind it.

This PR replaces the 2-D grid with a 1-D grid of `get_vectorcore_num()`
programs, each owning a contiguous range of the flattened `(token,
vocab_tile)` work space. The number of programs no longer depends on the
batch size or the vocabulary, and no helper is needed to choose it.

Here is the same launch before and after. `[8, 154880]` means
`num_vocab_blocks = 38`, so the old rule launched 304 programs and the
new one launches 48:

| kernel_details metric | before | after | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Duration** | **92.10 µs** | **46.58 µs** | **1.98× faster** |
| `aiv_time` | 80.512 µs | 32.408 µs | 2.48× less |
| `aiv_total_cycles` | 7 149 424 | 2 877 795 | 2.48× less |
| **`aiv_scalar_time`** | **66.788 µs** | **16.168 µs** | **4.13× less**
|
| `aiv_scalar_ratio` | 0.830 | 0.499 | - |
| **`aiv_vec_time`** | **8.834 µs** | **8.128 µs** | **unchanged** |
| `aiv_vec_ratio` | 0.110 | 0.251 | - |
| `aiv_mte2_time` | 4.062 µs | 3.075 µs | 1.32× less |
| `aiv_mte3_time` | 1.235 µs | 1.249 µs | unchanged |
| `aiv_icache_miss_rate` | 0.001 | 0.004 | - |

**The vector time does not move: 8.834 → 8.128 µs.** The same elements
get the same arithmetic whatever the grid is. Every microsecond
recovered came out of the scalar pipe, which is what the change is
designed to do. The kernel goes from 83 % scalar / 11 % vector to 50 %
scalar / 25 % vector, i.e. from overhead-dominated towards
work-dominated.

Over the whole profiled run (18 launches of this operator):

| op_statistic | before | after | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Count | 18 | 18 | - |
| **Total time** | **1504.50 µs** | **789.50 µs** | **1.91× less** |
| Avg time | 83.583 µs | 43.861 µs | 1.91× less |
| Min time | 19.98 µs | 19.60 µs | unchanged |
| Max time | 93.34 µs | 54.12 µs | 1.72× less |
| **Share of device time** | **1.715 %** | **0.907 %** | -0.81 pt |

Min time barely moves (19.98 → 19.60 µs), which is expected: those are
the small-batch launches where the old grid was already near-optimal and
there is little per-program cost to amortise. The gain is concentrated
in the larger calls.

**Scope, stated plainly:** this operator was 1.7 % of device time and is
now 0.9 %. It is a sampling-stage kernel, so roughly 1 % of device time
is the entire size of the prize.

### How the work is split

Tiles are numbered flat: tile `t` is token row `t // num_vocab_blocks`,
vocab block `t % num_vocab_blocks`. Program `p` owns `[p·per,
min((p+1)·per, total))` where `per = cdiv(total_tiles, num_workers)`,
converts that range to row bounds once with two integer divisions, and
then nests a row loop over a tile loop. Per-token scalar metadata is
read in the row loop, not the tile loop.

A contiguous range rather than the more obvious grid-stride (`for t in
range(pid, total, num_workers)`) because with 48 workers and 38 blocks
per row the stride is congruent to 2 mod 38, so consecutive iterations
land in different token rows and the per-token scalar reads would be
redone on every tile.

That programs are what cost time can be read off two measured points
without any model. `g` does not change how much vocabulary work there is
- every token row covers all 38 blocks either way - it changes only how
many programs that work is split across:

| `num_tokens` | programs at `g = 38` | µs | programs at `g = 1` | µs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 608 | 309.9 | 16 | 275.9 |
| 48 | 1 824 | 555.1 | 48 | 279.9 |
| 128 | 4 864 | 1 182.3 | 128 | 481.5 |
| 192 | 7 296 | 1 673.2 | 192 | 580.7 |

Identical work, 38× the programs, up to 2.9× the time. The old grid is
the one that pays the per-program cost the maximum number of times.

Fitting `time = waves × (P + B × blocks_per_program)` over 118 measured
`(num_tokens, g)` points gives a per-program cost **`P = 7.6 µs`**
against a per-tile cost of **`B = 2.6 µs`** on A2, so a one-block
program, which is what the old grid launched, spent most of its life in
cost that is independent of how many tiles it processes.

**What that per-program cost consists of is not established, and this PR
does not claim to know.** What is measured: it is 95-98 % scalar-pipe
work; it is paid only by programs that enter the vectorised loop body,
since a launch where every program reads the penalty metadata and then
early-returns costs 0.03-0.25 µs per program; `aiv_icache_miss_rate` is
~0.001, which rules out instruction-cache fill; and about 82 % of it
scales with `BLOCK_SIZE` (`P ≈ 1.3 µs + 1.42 ns/element × BLOCK_SIZE`),
so it is not a fixed prologue and it is not the per-token metadata
reads. The change does not depend on the answer: whatever it is made of,
it is paid once per program, so launching fewer programs is faster.

**The split deliberately carries no tuned constant, because the cost it
would encode is platform-specific.** Matched at `k_spec = 3`, the same
fit gives `P = 7.33 µs, B = 3.55 µs` on A2 against `P = 0.104 µs, B =
2.29 µs` on A5: the per-program cost is ~70× lower on A5 while the
per-tile cost moves only 1.55×, so A5 is not scalar-bound and the two
platforms differ in code generation rather than throughput. A variant
that picked a 2-D grid from a cost model fitted on A2 was measured and
is not in this PR: at `num_tokens` 24 and 48 on A5 it chooses a grid
with 1.27× the ideal tile count and lands 14-17 % **slower than main**.
The flat split minimises tiles on the critical path, which is the right
objective under either regime, and it measures at 1.01-1.10× of main on
A5 and never below 1.0.

Measured on the `apply_penalties` call on A2, 48 vector cores,
`vocab_size = 151936` (medians; these include the ~175 µs constant host
launch overhead, which this PR does not address, so the ratios here are
diluted at small batch where the profiler's are not):

| `num_tokens` | main (µs) | this PR (µs) | speedup | speedup, `k_spec =
3` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 257.4 | 216.9 | 1.19× | 1.12× |
| 16 | 315.5 | 233.9 | 1.35× | 1.27× |
| 32 | 451.4 | 277.8 | 1.63× | 1.56× |
| 64 | 692.6 | 342.2 | 2.02× | 1.83× |
| 128 | 1188.2 | 478.1 | 2.49× | 2.29× |
| 192 | 1692.8 | 619.8 | 2.73× | 2.64× |
| 256 | 2214.9 | 788.9 | **2.81×** | 2.62× |

On specialization: the kernel keeps `NUM_VOCAB_BLOCKS` and `BLOCK_SIZE`
as `tl.constexpr`, since both are fixed per model and shape the loops,
and passes the batch-dependent values (`vocab_size`, `total_tiles`,
`tiles_per_worker`) as runtime arguments. That is one compiled variant
rather than one per batch-size class: sweeping 40 batch sizes produces
no compilation after the first, and a 150-step trace with the batch size
changing every step adds nothing on a second pass. There is no warmup
for this path - `model_executor/warmup/penalties_triton_warmup.py` warms
the v1 sampler in `ops/triton/penalty.py`, not this kernel - so a
variant whose `tl.constexpr` set moves with the batch size would compile
during serving rather than at start-up. A unit test asserts the
constexpr set, so this cannot regress silently.

Net effect on the file: `_vocab_grid_size`, `_FIXED_COST_BLOCKS`,
`_MAX_CORE_DIM` and its assert, and the `functools` import all go, and
the kernel ends up smaller than it is on main.

`BLOCK_SIZE` is promoted to a module-level `VOCAB_BLOCK_SIZE` so tests
can launch the kernel with a matching tile width. On A2, 8192 overflows
UB at compile time, and 1024 and 2048 are measurably slower, so 4096
stays; A5 has more UB available and 8192 compiles there, which is left
for a follow-up since `get_ub_size_bytes()` cannot currently detect it.
`bincount()` keeps its own local `BLOCK_SIZE = 1024`, hence the distinct
name.

`get_vectorcore_num()` is read without calling
`init_device_properties_triton()` first, matching `min_p`, `logprob` and
`bad_words`; the worker initialises device properties at start-up
(`worker.py:489`).

Part of #14157. The issue lists several candidate optimisations; the
measurements above identify the grid as the one that is actually costing
time, so this PR changes only that. The rest are listed at the end.

### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change?

No. Output is bit-identical. The kernel's result does not depend on how
the `(token, vocab_tile)` space is partitioned, because every tile is
read, updated and stored by exactly one program with no cross-program
communication and no atomics. That the split is an exact partition is
checked over 2448 combinations of `num_tokens`, `vocab_size`, worker
count and tile width, and the kernel's output is asserted bit-identical
to the current implementation at every benchmarked point and at every
worker count the tests exercise.

### How was this patch tested?

Before this PR the operator tests only parametrised `VOCAB_SIZE =
[1000]`, a single 4096-wide vocab block, so the multi-block path and the
grid-stride loop were never exercised at all. Coverage is added in two
layers, and the two tests that already existed are unchanged.

A CPU unit test, `tests/ut/worker/v2/test_penalties.py` (23 cases),
which needs no NPU and therefore runs on every push via `cpu-ut` without
a label. It replaces `_penalties_kernel` with a fake that records the
launch, and asserts the grid is the core count independent of batch
size, that `total_tiles` and `tiles_per_worker` match the vocabulary
blocking, that `num_tokens == 0` returns without launching, that
replaying the kernel's loops over the split the launcher actually chose
covers every tile exactly once, and that the `tl.constexpr` set is
exactly `{NUM_VOCAB_BLOCKS, BLOCK_SIZE}` with the batch-dependent
arguments left at runtime.

Operator correctness on device, in
`tests/e2e/nightly/single_node/ops/singlecard_ops/triton/test_penality.py`:

- `test_apply_penalties_multi_vocab_block`: `vocab_size` in `{12800,
151936, 16384}` × `num_tokens` in `{1, 64}` × `num_speculative_tokens`
in `{0, 3}` × `{bf16, fp32}`, against the torch reference. The first two
have a partial tail block and 16384 is an exact multiple of the tile
width, so both mask paths are compared against the reference rather than
only launched.
- `test_apply_penalties_worker_invariance`: launches the kernel directly
at worker counts `{1, 7, num_vocab_blocks, 100}` with and without
speculative decoding, and asserts `torch.equal` between them. One count
per shape of the split: everything on one worker, coprime with the
blocks per row so workers start and end mid-row, exactly row-aligned,
and more workers than tiles. Speculative decoding is included because
`start_idx = token_idx - pos` reaches backwards across token rows, which
is where a mid-row split would corrupt a neighbouring request.
- `test_apply_penalties_penalty_configs`: every penalty combination, at
4 blocks without speculative decoding and again at 38 blocks with it.
One of them is a batch where half the requests have no penalty at all,
which is the case that exercises skipping a row and continuing; the
pre-existing randomised test reaches it only about 7 % of the time per
request.
- **Operator accuracy, before vs after**: on A5 and A3, 480 cases: {1,
5, 64, 256, 2048} tokens × {12800, 16384, 151936} vocab × {0, 3}
speculative tokens × all eight penalty configurations, in BF16 and FP32.
Output is bitwise identical to the pre-optimization kernel in every
case, and all 480 meet the reference accuracy standard against a float32
PyTorch reference (mixed tolerance `|actual - golden| <= atol + rtol *
|golden|`, requiring both ≥99% of elements within tolerance and max
absolute error within the per-dtype limit); 0 failures.

#### Test execution results

```

23 passed in 0.77s
>> pytest ./tests/e2e/nightly/single_node/ops/singlecard_ops/triton/test_penality.py
44 passed, 25 skipped in 48.98s
```

torch_npu=2.10.0.post7, triton_ascend=3.6.0.post2

```
23 passed in 0.22s
>> pytest ./tests/e2e/nightly/single_node/ops/singlecard_ops/triton/test_penality.py
69 passed in 73.83s
>> pytest ./tests/e2e/nightly/single_node/ops/singlecard_ops/triton/test_bincount.py::test_bincount_then_apply_penalties
2 passed in 11.03s
```

Tested on vllm-ascend@28e9e97ba254b07, CANN=9.2.1, torch=2.10.0+cpu,
torch_npu=2.10.0.post7, triton_ascend=3.6.0.post2

#### Performance validation (end-to-end serving)

Benchmarked on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-w8a8 with MTP speculative decoding (3
draft positions), 128 concurrent requests, and all three penalties
active (`frequency_penalty=0.1`, `presence_penalty=0.1`,
`repetition_penalty=1.1`) so `_penalties_kernel` is on the critical path
of every sampling step. Each request has a ~65.5K-token prompt (with 90%
prefix rate) and generates 1,024 tokens with `--ignore-eos`. Two runs
per configuration; hardware: A3 / 2 Cards / TP2.

| Metric (mean of 2 runs)        | Before | After  | Δ      |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | ------ | ------ |
| Mean TPOT (ms)                 | 128.99 | 125.62 | −2.6%  |
| Median TPOT (ms)               | 131.88 | 126.82 | −3.8%  |
| Mean ITL (ms)                  | 294.26 | 287.14 | −2.4%  |
| Median ITL (ms)                | 185.19 | 181.17 | −2.2%  |
| P99 ITL (ms)                   | 738.92 | 724.23 | −2.0%  |
| Total token throughput (tok/s) | 37,528 | 37,086 | −1.2%  |
| Acceptance rate (%)            | 42.8   | 42.9   | ±0.2pp |
| Acceptance length              | 2.29   | 2.29   | 0      |

The change only affects the sampling path, so per-output-token latency
is the metric it can move, and that is where the improvement shows up:
mean and median TPOT and ITL improve by 2–4%, and every individual
"after" run is better than every individual "before" run on those four
metrics (no overlap between the runs of the two configurations). This
matches what the kernel change predicts for exactly this regime — with
128 requests × 4 token positions per step, the old 2D grid launched one
program per (token, vocab-block) pair, thousands of them, each repeating
the same scalar penalty-parameter loads; the new 1D grid launches one
program per vector core and loads those scalars once per token row, so
the win grows with batch size and is a no-op for small batches.
Speculative-decoding acceptance rate, acceptance length, and
per-position acceptance are unchanged, confirming the optimization does
not alter sampling behaviour.

### Specialization analysis

`apply_penalties` keeps its signature, so callers and the `patch_v2`
override are unaffected. Internally the grid goes from `(rows,
vocab_grid)` to `(vectorcore_num,)`, `VOCAB_GRID_SIZE` is gone, and
`total_tiles` / `tiles_per_worker` arrive as runtime ints. Two new entry
conditions: `num_tokens == 0` returns before launching, and the launcher
reads `get_vectorcore_num()`, which needs
`init_device_properties_triton()` (done in `AscendWorker.init_device`).

| Argument | Before | After | Moves with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `NUM_VOCAB_BLOCKS`, `BLOCK_SIZE` | constexpr | constexpr | model vocab
/ fixed |
| `VOCAB_GRID_SIZE` | constexpr `min(blocks, 65535//rows)` | removed |
batch, above ~1074 rows |
| `total_tiles`, `tiles_per_worker` | — | runtime int | batch |
| `vocab_size`, strides | runtime int | runtime int | model only |

Only tile geometry stays compile-time: every distinct `tl.constexpr`
value compiles its own kernel, so batch-dependent values must stay
runtime. `tests/ut/worker/v2/test_penalties.py` asserts exactly that
set.

Measured with a custom script (Triton's `jit_cache_hook`, split by
phase; GPQA-style waves of 1–128 requests, all three penalties active):
59 distinct row counts collapse to **one specialization class**, with
**0 compiles at startup and 1 on the first penalised request**, nothing
warms this kernel under MRV2, since `kernel_warmup` warms the V1 kernel

baseline: the removed `VOCAB_GRID_SIZE` only varied above ~1074 rows,
which 128 requests with 3 MTP draft positions (512 rows) never reaches.

[Feature][Worker] Support Weight Checker on Ascend NPU (#18500)

## Purpose

This PR adds Ascend NPU support for the Weight Checker introduced in
[vLLM PR #51350](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51350) ([RFC
#52689](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52689)).

During RL training, weight updates must reach every rollout worker
correctly. Missing or partially applied updates can cause inconsistent
rollout weights and off-policy training. Weight Checker helps validate
the update path by computing model-parameter checksums, resetting
parameters, and comparing the restored weights against a known baseline.

The upstream vLLM implementation already provides `POST
/weight_checker`, frontend/engine dispatch, and checksum utilities. This
PR integrates the existing functionality into the Ascend NPU worker
without duplicating upstream APIs or engine logic.

## Design

**1. NPU worker integration**

Add the following methods to `NPUWorker` in
`vllm_ascend/worker/worker.py`:

- `compute_weight_checksums()`: compute SHA-256 digests using upstream
`compute_tensor_digests()` and return rank-prefixed parameter names.
- `reset_weights()`: zero model parameters using upstream
`zero_weights()` while leaving buffers unchanged.
- `_weight_checksum_prefix()`: generate unique
`dp{dp}:pp{pp}:pcp{pcp}:tp{tp}:` prefixes using `data_parallel_index`
and PP/PCP/TP rank information.
- `_weight_checksum_model()`: obtain the model from either
`model_runner.get_model()` or `model_runner.model` for compatibility
with different runner interfaces.

The existing `collective_rpc` mechanism dispatches these methods to the
workers. `NPUWorker310` inherits the implementation, although 310P
hardware has not been validated in this PR.

**2. Upstream reuse and version compatibility**

`NPUWorker` directly imports `compute_tensor_digests()` and
`zero_weights()` from vLLM's `weight_checksum` module. The module first
appeared in `v0.31.1rc0`; older versions cannot import `NPUWorker`, even
when Weight Checker is unused.

The current checkout selects vLLM main commit
`24420b7a341af37a9bc3186e6fc6062512e0aa58` and release tag `v0.33.0`.
For PRs targeting main, CPU unit-test CI covers both references; NPU
jobs use the verified main commit by default and also include the
release tag when `main2main` is enabled.

The validation reported below used the verified main commit. It does not
claim a locally completed validation run against `v0.33.0`. This PR adds
no package-level minimum version constraint or runtime guard.

**3. Ascend-specific recovery behavior**

RL configurations automatically disable `weight_nz_mode`, so the
standard RL weight-update path is unaffected. When `weight_nz_mode` is
enabled explicitly, resetting weights emits a warning because the
weight-transfer update path is unavailable in that configuration.
Recovery through `reload_weights()` remains possible where supported.
Users must ensure that a valid recovery path exists before resetting the
parameters.

**4. Tests and documentation**

- Worker unit tests: `tests/ut/worker/test_worker_weight_checker.py`.
- Weight Checker E2E tests:
`tests/e2e/pull_request/two_card/rlhf/state_transitions/test_weight_checker.py`,
with shared helpers under `tests/e2e/common/rlhf/`.
- User documentation: `docs/source/user_guide/feature_guide/rl.md`.

The guide now includes explicit server/trainer device selection, a
trainer example that restores the original checkpoint over HCCL while
keeping generation paused, checks before and after restoration, and
conditional resume after a full checksum match. It also documents
prerequisites and automated validation commands.

With a compatible upstream vLLM and `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1`, users can
invoke the existing Weight Checker development endpoint on Ascend NPU:

| Request | Response | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{"action": "checksum"}` | `{"checksums": {key: sha256_hex}}` |
Capture the current parameter checksums |
| `{"action": "reset"}` | `{"status": "reset"}` | Zero the covered model
parameters |
| `{"action": "compare", "baseline": {key: sha256_hex}}` | `{"match":
bool, "mismatches": [key]}` | Identify changed or missing parameters |

Recommended verification workflow:

1. Pause inference and capture the checksum baseline.
2. Reset the rollout worker parameters.
3. Restore the **same expected weights** through NPU IPC, HCCL weight
transfer, or `reload_weights()`.
4. Compare against the baseline, verify `match: true`, and resume
inference.

If the trainer has performed a genuine optimization step, the new
weights should not be compared with an old baseline. The baseline must
correspond to the expected weight version.

**Limitations:** As in upstream vLLM, buffers, draft models, and LoRA
adapters are outside the Weight Checker coverage. Quantized/MoE models,
PP/PCP configurations, and 310P hardware were not validated in this
acceptance run. Basic and TP/DP checksum cases use eager mode; IPC/HCCL
transfer cases use the shared RLHF helper's `FULL_DECODE_ONLY`
configuration with capture size 1. Other graph configurations are
outside the claimed automated-test coverage. The development endpoint is
destructive when `reset` is called and should not be exposed to
untrusted clients.

## Test Plan

The test categories follow the [upstream vLLM Weight Checker
PR](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51350): unit tests for
worker/checksum behavior and E2E tests for API behavior, weight
recovery, and distributed-worker coverage. The E2E scenarios live in a
single file whose single-rank lanes use one NPU and whose multi-rank
lanes use two.

**Unit tests (worker integration)**

- Verify that the Weight Checker methods are available on the Ascend
worker classes.
- Verify unique checksum prefixes across dense DP replicas and valid
parameter-name/digest formatting.
- Verify that `reset_weights()` zeros parameters without modifying
buffers.
- Verify that `reset_weights()` warns when `weight_nz_mode` is enabled.
- Verify model lookup with both supported ModelRunner interfaces.
- Run the related HCCL weight-transfer engine tests.

These complement the upstream checksum-utility tests for tensor layouts,
parameter subclasses, and shared parameters; those upstream utility
cases are not reimplemented in vllm-ascend.

**E2E tests (Weight Checker workflow)**

- **API validation:** invalid requests return HTTP 400; `checksum` is
stable; `compare` detects modified and missing baseline keys.
- **Reset and checkpoint recovery:** resetting weights produces
mismatches; `reload_weights()` restores a full match.
- **Weight transfer recovery:** resetting and restoring through real NPU
IPC and HCCL weight transfers produces a full match, including packed
and unpacked transfer modes.
- **Distributed coverage:** TP=2 and DP=2 tests verify that every worker
rank is included in checksums and reset/reload, and that missing-rank
entries are detected.

The NZ-mode warning path is covered by a unit test rather than a
dedicated E2E lane, because RL configurations disable NZ mode
automatically. Upstream route tests are not duplicated because this PR
does not change the frontend routes. The E2E suite requires a paired
vLLM containing the Weight Checker API; it does not skip automatically
when that API is unavailable.

Run from the vllm-ascend repository root on a compatible Ascend NPU
environment:

```bash
bash format.sh ci
python -m pytest -q \
  tests/ut/worker/test_worker_weight_checker.py \
  tests/ut/distributed/weight_transfer/test_hccl_engine.py
python -m pytest -sv -ra \
  tests/e2e/pull_request/two_card/rlhf/state_transitions/test_weight_checker.py
```

## Test Result

**Environment:** Ascend 950DT NPUs; Python 3.12.13; CANN 9.2.0; PyTorch
2.10.0; torch_npu 2.10.0.post7; full 28-layer Qwen3-0.6B architecture.

Validation used:

- vLLM: `24420b7a341af37a9bc3186e6fc6062512e0aa58`
- vllm-ascend: `4e206b3f6be8a4580ea74f8ff9b2c8a0a12f291d`

| Test category | Passed | Failed | Skipped |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Weight Checker worker unit tests | 6 | 0 | 0 |
| HCCL weight-transfer unit tests | 37 | 0 | 0 |
| Weight Checker E2E tests | 12 | 0 | 0 |
| **Total** | **55** | **0** | **0** |

The E2E run completed in 471.13 seconds using up to two NPUs. All cases
passed, including API validation, checksum/reset/reload, packed and
unpacked NPU IPC/HCCL transfers, and TP=2/DP=2 rank coverage.

Basic and TP/DP cases use checkpoint-loaded weights and eager mode.
IPC/HCCL cases start with dummy weights, receive fixed-random weights
through the trainer API, and validate reset/restoration using the same
weight source. These transfer cases use `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` with capture
size 1.

**Manual guide validation:** The documented server command was also
exercised without adding `--enforce-eager`. A separate trainer loaded
the original Qwen3-0.6B checkpoint. The workflow captured 226 checksum
entries, detected 226 mismatches after reset, restored the original
weights through HCCL, and returned `{"match":true,"mismatches":[]}`.
After resume, generation succeeded and the deterministic sample output
matched the pre-reset output.

The manual run used an auxiliary trainer harness based on the linked
HCCL example to keep generation paused until comparison completed. The
guide was subsequently updated to include this missing orchestration.

**Current-head qualification:** Commit
`f7084ee2a0c7ac01e2463d011dd2f156004656fb` only updates the
documentation; implementation and test code are unchanged from the
validated commit. The revised documentation's Python, Bash, and JSON
examples passed syntax checks, and `git diff --check` passed. The final
revised guide has not been rerun verbatim.

**Remaining validation limits:** No quantized/MoE, PP/PCP, or 310P
validation is claimed. Full repository test coverage and arbitrary graph
configurations are not claimed. `bash format.sh ci` could not run
locally because `pre-commit` was unavailable; no successful
full-format-check result is claimed.

commits.message: [Feature][MRV2] Support LM head TP with probabilistic draft sampling (#21209) ### What this PR does / why we need it? Enable LM head TP together with `draft_sample_method="probabilistic"` in Model Runner V2. Previously, the shared draft wrapper padded hidden states before calling upstream `sample_draft` and only trimmed the sampled token IDs afterward. Probabilistic sampling would therefore consume extra logits rows without corresponding request metadata, risking invalid mapping reads and draft-logits cache writes; the combination was rejected. Move alignment into `LmheadTPDraftSamplingMixin.compute_draft_logits`: pad hidden states for the LM-head collectives, then trim logits back to the original input row count **before** upstream sampling. This preserves original graph-padding rows and DFlash's multiple rows per request while keeping LM-head-only padding out of the sampler. - Enable probabilistic sampling for MTP, Eagle, Gemma4 MTP and DFlash through the shared hook. - Allow DSpark through initialization validation; its existing model-level pad/trim path already trims before its independent sampling flow and remains unchanged. - Preserve rejection of DFlash2/LiLiCorr and the local-argmax/adaptive-verification restrictions. Standalone AR and multi-module MTP do not inherit this hook. - Keep upstream vLLM code and sampling kernels unchanged. ### Does this PR introduce _any_ user-facing change? Yes. Users can combine LM head TP with probabilistic draft sampling for the supported algorithms above. The existing greedy sampling path remains covered.
